title: Doomed from the Start: Predicting Agent Failure Before It Happens
hook: An agent that's going to fail often shows it in its hidden activations from round one — long before its actual behavior looks any different. Reading that signal saves nearly half the compute.
key_points: LLM agents on multi-step tasks often commit to doomed trajectories early, but keep consuming inference compute long before the failure becomes visible.
Lightweight probes on hidden activations predict eventual failure as early as the first interaction round — scorers reading only observable behavior are barely better than chance at that point.
Turns the signal into an abort cascade: one calibrated gate per round, with per-round recall budgets tuned so successful episodes survive at a chosen global rate.
At a 90% recall target, saves 47.1% ± 10.3% of inference compute on Qwen-2.5-7B and 37.2% ± 8.8% on Llama-3.2-3B — 1.6-1.7x more than the best single-gate policy.
Adding behavioral features to the probe adds nothing further: the hidden states already capture everything behavior reveals, and more.
content_html: Watching an LLM agent's outputs, a doomed trajectory often looks fine for a while — right up until it obviously isn't. This paper's core claim is that the doom was visible internally the whole time, just not in what the agent said or did.
extra_html: The authors train lightweight per-round probes on an agent's hidden activations and find they can anticipate eventual episode failure as early as the first interaction round, at a point where scorers reading only the agent's observable behavior are barely better than chance. They turn this into a practical abort cascade: one distribution-free, calibrated gate per round, with per-round recall budgets jointly searched so that episodes that would have eventually succeeded survive every gate at a user-chosen global rate — because false-abort risk compounds across gates, and that episode-level guarantee is the one that actually matters in deployment. Across two agent models on TextCraft, the cascade hits every recall target from 90% to 97%, and at the 90% target saves 47.1% ± 10.3% of inference compute on Qwen-2.5-7B and 37.2% ± 8.8% on Llama-3.2-3B — 1.6 to 1.7 times more than the best single-gate policy. A behavior-only version of the same cascade saves roughly half as much, and layering behavioral features onto the hidden-state probe adds nothing further: the hidden states already capture what behavior reveals, and more. The paper also characterizes exactly how much data is needed to certify a given recall target — telling practitioners which promises their data can, and provably cannot, back up. Kai Ruan and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Token Budgets: When Agents Burn Money
related.hook: A single retry loop can spend thousands of dollars before anyone notices. This paper catalogs 63 real budget-overrun incidents — and asks the type system to make over-spending a compile error.

related.title: Plans Don't Persist: Context Management Is Load-Bearing for Agents
related.hook: An agent writes a plan, then context compression evicts it. This paper shows the plan never became internal state — once it leaves the window, the agent forgets it and task success craters.

related.title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
related.hook: Full agentic evals like SWE-Bench and GAIA can cost thousands of dollars and days to run — PACE predicts those scores from a tiny, cheap subset of ordinary benchmarks, at under 1% of the cost.

flashcards.prompt: What's the key finding about when an agent's eventual failure becomes predictable?
flashcards.back_html: Failure is predictable from the agent's internal hidden activations as early as the first interaction round — well before it's visible from the agent's observable behavior alone.

flashcards.prompt: What happens when the authors add behavioral features on top of the hidden-state probe?

choices.text: No further gain — the hidden states already capture everything the behavioral features reveal
Accuracy improves dramatically, showing behavior matters more than hidden states
The probe becomes unusable due to added noise
It only helps on one of the two tested models

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper reports that an otherwise-identical cascade reading only behavior saves roughly half as much compute, and stacking behavioral features onto the hidden-state probe adds no further gain — the hidden states already capture what behavior reveals.
